passage:
Back at the school hostel after the science trip, the Class 10 girls kept retelling the bus breakdown. "The driver shouted at the mechanic," Ishita said. "And smoke poured out of the engine," someone added. "We had to walk to the dhaba in the dark."
Aditi had been asleep for most of it, headphones on. But by the third night of retelling, she was adding, "I saw the smoke. It was grey and smelled like burnt rubber."
When the warden showed the trip photos, there was no smoke, and it was still light when they walked. Aditi looked at the screen, confused. "But I remember it," she whispered.
Ishita said, "Honestly, I think I added the smoke too."

qa.q: What was Aditi doing during most of the breakdown?
qa.a: Aditi had been asleep for most of it, headphones on.

qa.q: Why did Aditi whisper, "But I remember it"?
qa.a: Hearing the story three nights in a row made the smoke and the dark feel like her own memories, so the photos felt strange to her.

qa.q: What could the group do to keep shared stories more accurate?
qa.a: They could check photos early, as the warden did, and say "I didn't see that myself" when repeating someone else's detail.

qa.q: What does Ishita's admission suggest about the others' memories?
qa.a: If even Ishita added the smoke, the group's retelling changed everyone's version, not only Aditi's.

grounding: It shows a teenager who absorbs friends' retellings of a shared trip and comes to remember things she never saw.

passage:
Dear Varun,
Something weird happened with the football match story. You know how everyone keeps telling it at lunch: the referee's whistle breaking, you slipping in the mud, Coach laughing so hard he had to sit down?
Yesterday I told it to my cousin with all those bits, as if I'd seen them. Then my cousin said, "Weren't you in the washroom for the second half?" I was! I missed the whole thing. I have no idea whether the whistle broke or whether Coach sat down. I've heard it so many times that it feels like I watched it.
So I'm asking you: what actually happened? I'll trust your version over mine for now.
Pema

qa.q: Where was Pema during the second half?
qa.a: Pema was in the washroom for the second half.

qa.q: Why did Pema tell the story like an eyewitness?
qa.a: Hearing it again and again at lunch made the whistle and the mud feel like things Pema had watched, so it seemed like a real memory.

qa.q: What choice does Pema make at the end, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Pema asks Varun what actually happened and decides to trust that version for now, since Varun was really on the field.

qa.q: How might Varun feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Varun might laugh at being asked, but also value Pema's honesty and take care to separate what Varun truly saw from what others added.

grounding: It shows a teenager who realises that friends' repeated retellings of a match have become a personal memory of events never seen.

passage:
Okay, Parul, is this recording? Good. My strange memory is from the terrace, two winters ago. A group of us were lighting sparklers, and a spark landed on Neel's sleeve. Everyone tells it the same way: he yelled, jumped into a bucket of water, and the bucket tipped over.
I told that story for a year. I could see the bucket rolling. Then Neel himself told me, "There was no bucket. I just shook my arm and it went out." And I thought, no, I remember the bucket! But when I checked, I'd gone downstairs for matches right then.
The bucket came from Joel's version. It moved into my head and sat there like mine.
Now I say, "I heard that..." if I didn't see it. I'm Vasudha, by the way.

qa.q: Where had Vasudha gone at the moment the spark fell?
qa.a: Vasudha had gone downstairs for matches right then.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha feel sure about the rolling bucket?
qa.a: Vasudha had told the story for a year and could see the bucket, even though it came from Joel's version; repeating it made the detail feel owned.

qa.q: What habit did Vasudha adopt, and why does it help?
qa.a: Vasudha says "I heard that..." when not an eyewitness, which keeps borrowed details apart from real memories.

qa.q: How might Neel feel hearing the bucket story told for a year?
qa.a: Neel might be amused or a little annoyed, since the story made his moment more dramatic than it was and nobody asked him.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose memory of a shared incident took on a detail that only a friend had described.

passage: I'm Tanuja, Nikita's older sister. Nikita's class went to Bhimtal lake last month. Nikita was in the second boat with her friend Pooja; the drama happened in the first boat. I know because Nikita phoned me that night: "Didi, did you hear? A snake swam next to Juhi's boat and Mohan almost fell in!" Since then her friends have told the story at our house twice, louder each time, the snake getting longer. Yesterday Nikita told our cousins, "The snake swam right past me, and I grabbed Mohan's shirt so he wouldn't fall." She said it with total certainty, eyes wide. I reminded her she was in the second boat. She frowned. "No, I was there. I can see its head in the water." I don't think she's lying. I think she's heard it so often it's become hers.

qa.q: Which boat was Nikita in?
qa.a: The second boat, with her friend Pooja.

qa.q: How does Nikita feel about being in the snake story, and what shows it?
qa.a: Nikita feels completely sure and excited, telling it with wide eyes and frowning when reminded she was in the second boat, because her friends' retellings blended into her memory.

qa.q: How could Tanuja help Nikita without calling her a liar?
qa.a: Tanuja could explain that group stories often blend into our own memories, and suggest asking Pooja what the second boat actually saw.

qa.q: How might Mohan feel hearing Nikita say she grabbed his shirt?
qa.a: Mohan might be confused, since he remembers no one from the other boat grabbing him, and may wonder where the detail came from.

grounding: A sister watches a teenager come to remember a boat incident she only heard friends describe, as group retelling blends into her memory.

passage:
Wednesday: The fire alarm rang during chemistry lab. Rukmini, fifteen, was in the washroom down the corridor and came out to find everyone lined up on the field. Aparna whispered, "A test tube cracked on the burner. Smoke everywhere."
Thursday: At lunch the story grew. "It was a small explosion," someone said. "Glass flew," said another. "Sir's eyebrows got singed!" Everyone laughed. Rukmini laughed too, picturing it.
Monday: At dinner Rukmini told her mother, "I was right there when the test tube blew up. A bit of glass hit my sleeve." Her mother looked alarmed. Aparna, visiting, put down her spoon. "Rukku, you were in the washroom." Rukmini opened her mouth to argue, then stopped. She could see the glass. She just couldn't remember seeing it.

qa.q: Where was Rukmini when the fire alarm rang?
qa.a: In the washroom down the corridor.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini feel sure, at dinner, that she had seen the glass?
qa.a: She pictured it while laughing with her friends, and that imagined picture blended into her memory until it felt like her own.

qa.q: What did Rukmini do when Aparna corrected her, and why was that a good choice?
qa.a: She stopped instead of arguing, which let her notice that she could picture the scene but not actually remember seeing it.

qa.q: What is it like for Aparna to hear Rukmini retell a scene she missed?
qa.a: Aparna is startled enough to put down her spoon; she knows where Rukmini really was, so she has to speak up gently and correct a friend in front of her mother.

grounding: Over several days, a teenager who missed a lab incident absorbs her friends' retellings and comes to remember being there.
